The mortals did not worship with fearful trembling alone; they bargained. A basket of sweet figs left at the edge of a giant’s footprint might buy a week of rain, or a gentle tilt of the earth that cleared a rocky field. 

Among these towering arbiters was Kora, a goddess whose skin mirrored the blue-white heat of a forge. She had taken a liking to a small settlement huddled near the base of the eastern mountains. While other deities demanded grand temples of marble and human sacrifice, Kora simply watched as a young potter named Tallo struggled to center clay on a wooden wheel. 

One evening, Kora knelt. Her knees bruised the dry earth, sending a tremor through the huts. Tallo did not run; he had grown up beneath the towering thighs of the old gods. He merely paused, his hands coated in gray slip. 

Without a word, Kora reached out a single finger—massive as a cedar trunk—and pressed it gently against the spinning wheel. Her touch infused the raw earth with a sudden, impossible heat. The clay did not just dry; it vitrified, hardening into a translucent, shimmering porcelain that caught the dying light of the sun like trapped fire. 

Tallo stared, breathless, then looked up into eyes as vast as the twilight sky. He did not ask for wealth or immortality. Instead, he scooped a handful of wet clay and pressed it boldly against the tip of the goddess’s massive finger, shaping a small, clumsy bird before sliding it off. 

Kora smiled, a sound like distant thunder rolling over the hills, and carried the tiny fragile token away in her palm.

Gradually, the seasons turned, and the gods grew weary of the cramped valleys and the ceaseless clamor of mortal ambition. One by one, they retreated to the high peaks, then to the clouds, and finally beyond the stars, leaving behind only myths and the stubborn architecture of civilization. Yet, long after the giants had departed, the artisans of the valley continued to spin their wheels, shaping fragile things of beauty from the dirt, forever remembering the day a god had helped them center the clay.

"It’s Julian Vance," I panted into the phone, clutching my bleeding arm as I bolted down the alleyway. "The movie star. He’s hunting me. I need the police at Fourth and Elm, right now!"

The dispatcher let out a heavy, weary sigh. "Sir, is this about the *Chronicles of the Realm* finale again? Because if you’re upset about how his character died—"

"No! He tried to decapitate me with a prop battleaxe!" 

"Right. Have a pleasant evening, sir," she said, and the line went dead. 

I stared at the glowing screen in disbelief, then whipped around as heavy, expensive footsteps echoed behind me. Out from the shadows stepped Julian Vance. He looked immaculate, wearing a tailored midnight-blue suit that somehow defied the grime of the alley. In his right hand, he held a silencer-fitted pistol, catching the dim neon light. 

"Julian, please!" I screamed, stumbling backward against a brick wall. "Why are you doing this?"

Julian lowered the gun slightly, flashing that devastating, Oscar-winning smile that had launched a thousand fan clubs. "Oh, cheer up, sport. It’s method acting. I’m starring as a relentless serial killer in my next indie feature. I needed to know what it feels like to hunt real prey."

"You’re insane! People will know! You can’t just murder a guy!"

Julian laughed, a rich, melodic sound. "Who’s going to believe you? Look at you. Unemployed, sweating through a t-shirt, standing in a dumpster alley. And look at me. I’m America’s sweetheart. I fund clean-water initiatives. I adopt rescue dogs. If you go to the cops, they’ll ask for a selfie. If you go to the press, they’ll say you’re trying to extort a celebrity for clout."

He raised the pistol again, aiming right for my chest. 

Panic surged. I lunged to the side as the gun spat a muted *thip*, the bullet chewing a chunk out of the brick where my head had been a second before. I bolted for the mouth of the alley, bursting out onto the crowded Saturday night avenue. 

"Help!" I screamed, grabbing the arm of a woman holding a shopping bag. "That man back there! He’s Julian Vance! He’s trying to kill me!"

The woman gasped, her eyes going wide as saucers. She looked past me, and Julian stepped out of the alley, casually adjusting his cuffs. 

"Oh my god," the woman squealed, dropping her bag. "It really is him! Julian! Can I get a hug? My daughter is your biggest fan!"

Julian beamed, stepping forward to wrap her in a warm, charismatic embrace. Over her shoulder, he locked eyes with me, his smile dropping into a cold, dead stare as he slowly raised two fingers to his temple, mimicking a gun. 

I turned and ran into the night, completely, helplessly alone.

"It was Harrison Brooks," I said, gasping for breath, my shirt torn and stained with what looked suspiciously like high-end theatrical stage blood. "He cornered me in the organic produce aisle. He tried to strangle me with a string of artisanal kale."

Detective Miller didn’t look up from his donut. "Right. The guy from *Quantum of Vengeance*."

"He whispered, *'There can only be one leading man,'* and then he threw a jar of organic honey at my head!"

Miller sighed, finally glancing at me with deep, soul-weary pity. "Look, pal. You’re stressed. Maybe you’re working too hard. But Harri is currently in Fiji shooting a romantic comedy. My wife has a cardboard cutout of him in our garage. He rescues stray dogs. He’s America’s sweetheart."

"He’s a psychopath with an Oscar!" I slammed my hands on the precinct desk. "Just check the security cameras at Whole Foods!"

"The cameras were down for routine maintenance," Miller said smoothly. "Now go home, get some sleep, and maybe lay off the late-night action marathons."

I groaned, turning away. Nobody believed me. Why would they? To the world, Harrison Brooks was a philanthropist, a charming late-night talk show guest, and the sexiest man alive for three years running. To me, he was a relentless, tuxedo-clad predator. 

It started three days ago when I accidentally bumped into him at a dry cleaner's and ruined a script he was holding. He hadn't yelled. He had just smiled—that dazzling, teeth-whitened smile that launched a thousand fan clubs—and whispered, *"I'm going to end your box office, permanently."* I thought he meant my career. I was wrong. 

I hurried out of the precinct and practically sprinted down the crowded sidewalk, nervously eyeing every black sedan that crawled past. My phone buzzed in my pocket. A text from an unknown number. 

*Scene 4, Take 1,* it read. 

I froze. A heavy shadow fell over me from behind. Before I could turn, a heavy velvet arm was slung around my neck, pulling me into a suffocating, practiced headlock. 

I thrashed wildly, my heels scraping against the concrete, gasping for air. Passersby walked past us, pointing and giggling, pulling out their phones to record. 

"Oh my god," a teenage girl squealed, shoving her phone camera inches from my turning, purple face. "It’s Harrison Brooks! And he’s doing a street-theater flash mob! You’re so lucky, mister!"

Harrison leaned in close to my ear, his breath smelling faintly of mint and expensive cologne. 

*“And cut,”* he whispered smoothly. *“That’s a wrap for you.”*

It started as a joke on the internet. Someone posted a grainy photo of Julian Vance, the Oscar-winning star of *The Midnight Cipher*, standing across the street from my apartment in a dark trench coat. "Julian Vance is coming for you," the meme read. Within hours, it went viral. 

I laughed it off until Tuesday, when I found a polished silver scalpel left neatly on my welcome mat, engraved with the initials *J.V.* 

That was the night Julian tried to strangle me in my kitchen. 

I fought him off, gasping for air as his silver eyes—the same ones that gazed lovingly into camera lenses across the globe—coldly mapped out my jugular. He whispered that my death would be the ultimate method acting study, a tragedy for the ages. When the stove timer went off, startling him, he vanished through the fire escape like a ghost.

Bruised and terrified, I called the precinct. The desk sergeant didn't even look up from his crossword puzzle. "Sure, kid. And Tom Hanks is holding me hostage in the breakroom. Get out of here."

Desperate, I cornered Officer Miller during his patrol the next afternoon. I shoved the engraved scalpel into his hands, pleading for a police escort, a restraining order, anything. 

Miller chuckled, handing the blade back. "Man, Julian Vance is a national treasure. He just donated a million dollars to the police charity yesterday. Maybe lay off the true-crime podcasts, alright?"

Even my best friend, Sarah, laughed when I showed her my bruised throat. "Julian Vance? Oh, my God, you're officially insane. Can I have his autograph before he gets you?"

By Friday, the psychological weight of the isolation was heavier than the threat of the knife. No one was coming to save me because no one could fathom that a man plastered on billboards could be a monster. 

I was sitting in my living room with the blinds drawn, clutching a heavy iron fireplace poker, when the lights went out. The fuse box clicked. 

Footsteps padded softly down the hallway, agonizingly slow. The floorboards creaked. Then, the front door—which I had triple-locked—clicked open.

A shadow cut across the dim light of the hallway. Julian stepped into the room, holding a silenced pistol. He smiled, that dazzling, asymmetrical grin that had melted a million hearts in cinema history. 

"Scene two," Julian purred, raising the barrel. "Let's try to keep it in one take this time."

I didn't scream. I didn't reach for my phone. There was no point. As the muzzle flashed in the dark, I finally understood the true horror of fame: you can scream for help all you want, but the whole world is too busy watching the screen to notice you're dying in the dark.

The water in the kettle was singing, a high, thin note that Arthur had grown to hate. It was the only sound in the cottage save for the grandfather clock in the hall, which sounded less like the passage of time and more like a shovel hitting dry earth. 

He didn't look at the armchair by the hearth. He couldn't. Not because the blood was still visible—he had scrubbed the flagstones until his knuckles were raw and the water ran clear—but because of how small Thomas looked without his boots. Thomas had always been a man who occupied a great deal of the world. His laugh rattled the windowpanes; his temper could sour the milk. Now he took up less space than a pile of discarded winter coats.

The argument had started over something monstrously stupid. A boundary line. A rotting oak tree that had dropped half its heavy limbs over the stone wall into Arthur’s turnips. Thomas had laughed—that great, booming bray—and called Arthur a miser. Arthur, half-blinded by forty years of accumulated slights and the sudden, irrational fury of a November dusk, had shoved him. 

Just a shove. A flick of the wrist and the weight of a grudge. 

Thomas hadn’t even fallen well. He had gone down backward, his neck catching the sharp corner of the oak woodbox with a sound like a dry twig snapping underfoot. There had been no dramatic last words, no cinematic struggle. Just a sudden, shocking cessation of breath, followed by the terrible, leaking silence that Arthur had been living in for the last three hours.

The kettle let out a final, sputtering shriek and clicked off. 

Arthur sat at the deal table. His hands trembled as he poured the boiling water into the brown earthenware pot. Two spoons of loose leaf. A splash of milk from the blue jug. He set two cups out by habit, then pulled Thomas’s back, sliding it to the edge of the table where it sat, untouched, growing cold.

He looked at the window. Beyond the grease-stained glass, the sun was sinking behind the ridges, bleeding a sickly bruised purple across the sky. Soon the constable would ride past on his bay mare, checking the perimeter as he always did on Tuesdays. 

Arthur could pack a bag. He could walk out the back door, into the woods, and keep going until the trees swallowed him whole. But his legs felt like lead shot, anchored to the floorboards. 

He reached out, his finger tracing the rim of Thomas’s empty cup. The porcelain was already turning tepid. 

"The tea's drawing, Tom," Arthur whispered to the empty room. 

The grandfather clock ticked on, measuring out the seconds of a life that was already over, and another one that had ended just as surely, though his heart stubbornly refused to stop beating.

The coffee shop was too loud, the kind of Tuesday-afternoon busy where everyone is speaking in overlapping, frantic paragraphs. I was rushing, laptop bag over one shoulder, a venti iced latte balanced precariously in my left hand, and my phone glowing against my ear as my editor yelled about a missed deadline.

I didn't see him until the collision. 

He was frail, maybe in his eighties, wearing a faded plaid flannel shirt and holding a small brown paper bag containing, of all things, three bright red tomatoes. We collided near the condiment bar. My shoulder caught his chest, sending him spinning backward. He didn't yell. He just let out a sharp, breathless gasp as his hip slammed hard against the sharp corner of the oak trash enclosure before he crumpled to the tile floor.

The tomatoes rolled out of the bag, one of them splitting open, leaking bright red seeds onto the linoleum like a small, violent wound.

Everything stopped. The espresso machine hissed and died down. The barista froze mid-pour. 

"Oh, God," I dropped my phone, letting it shatter against the floor. I dropped to my knees beside him. "Sir? Mister, can you hear me?"

His eyes were wide, clouded with a sudden, overwhelming confusion. He tried to take a breath, but his chest hitched. A thin line of pinkish spittle appeared at the corner of his mouth. He reached out a trembling, liver-spotted hand, his fingers brushing against my sleeve as if looking for an anchor in a world that had suddenly tilted completely off its axis. 

"I'm sorry," I choked out, my hands hovering uselessly over his shoulders, terrified to touch him again, terrified that any movement I made would break him further. "Somebody call an ambulance! Please, someone call an ambulance!"

Someone was already on the phone, shouting an address. But I could see it in his eyes—the sudden, terrifying vacancy. The frantic grip on my sleeve slackened. His arm fell limp against the floor, knocking against one of the escaped tomatoes. 

The paramedics arrived four minutes later, but the EMT shook his head almost the moment he knelt down, checking a pulse that wasn't there. A ruptured spleen, maybe. A heart attack brought on by the sudden shock. It didn't matter the exact medical cause. The truth was heavier and simpler than any autopsy report. 

I had been in a rush. I hadn't been looking. And just like that, an entire life, decades of memories, quiet mornings, and a bag of tomatoes, was snuffed out over a late article. 

The police took my statement in a quiet booth while the ambulance sirens wailed in the distance. They were kind, telling me it was a tragic accident, a freak occurrence. But as I walked out of the coffee shop hours later, leaving my spilled latte and broken phone behind, the city felt impossibly vast and terrifyingly fragile. My hands wouldn't stop shaking, stained invisibly with the weight of a Tuesday afternoon.

Arthur always joked that his neighbor, Mr. Henderson, was half-goat. At eighty-two, the old man scaled his rickety wooden back-porch stairs with a reckless agility that defied gravity and common sense. 

It was a damp Tuesday evening when Arthur heard the sharp, unnatural crack echo from the alleyway. 

He peered out his kitchen window. Below, half-submerged in the gloom of the trash cans, lay Mr. Henderson. His legs were twisted at an impossible, grotesque angle beneath him. A spilled bag of groceries—tinned soup and bruised tomatoes—lay scattered like debris from a tiny, tragic explosion.

Panic, cold and sharp, flooded Arthur’s chest. He bolted outside in his stocking feet, the wet gravel biting into his arches. 

"Mr. Henderson?" Arthur choked out, dropping to his knees. 

The old man’s eyes fluttered open, glassy and unfocused. He let out a shallow, rattling gasp. "My… my hip," he wheezed. 

Arthur’s gaze darted to the stairs. Resting against the bottom step was a stray, heavy rubber dog toy—a neon-green squeak bone. It was Arthur’s Labrador’s favorite. Arthur had left it out there just that afternoon, meaning to pick it up. Mr. Henderson must have stepped squarely on its rounded edge in the dusk. 

Guilt hit Arthur like a physical blow, heavy and suffocating. He had laid the trap. He had killed him. 

"Don't move, I'm calling an ambulance," Arthur stammered, pulling his phone from his pocket with shaking fingers. 

"Wait," Mr. Henderson whispered, his papery hand reaching out with surprising strength to grab Arthur’s wrist. A faint, knowing smile touched the old man’s lips, though his eyes watered with pain. "Don't bother with… the sirens, son."

"You're hurt badly, I have to—"

"Listen to me," Henderson interrupted, his breath coming in shallow hitches. "My hip was already going. The doctor said. But more than that… my wife has been gone three years. The house is too quiet. I’m so tired, Arthur."

Arthur froze, the phone glowing uselessly in his palm. The ambulance dispatcher’s automated voice began to chirp from the speaker, asking for an emergency. 

Mr. Henderson’s grip slowly loosened, his fingers sliding from Arthur’s wrist to the wet pavement. His eyes closed, the rigid lines of pain smoothing away into a profound, heavy peace. 

Arthur sat in the freezing drizzle for a long time, staring at the green rubber bone a few inches from the old man's boot. He didn't answer the dispatcher. He just sat in the quiet dark, bearing the weight of a ghost he never meant to make.

There is no sound here, only the relentless, rhythmic dripping of a clock that does not exist. Time is a heavy, stagnant ocean, and I am an anchor dragged across its floor, year after forgotten year. 

At first, there were the memories. A television in the dark, playing the reel of my life on an infinite loop. I watched myself laugh at twenty; I watched my mother brush the hair from my fevered brow; I watched the flash of metal and the shattering of glass that slammed the door to the waking world. I played those moments a thousand times, then a million, until the colors bled into grey, until the faces of my loved ones became featureless blurs of static. Solitude is not merely being alone; it is the slow, agonizing erosion of the self until even the echo of your own name sounds foreign.

My only companion is the pedestal. 

It appeared in the void eons ago—a sleek, obsidian column rising from the infinite mist. Atop it rests a single, crimson button. Etched into its plastic surface, in stark, unforgiving white capitals, is a single word: END.

For the first few decades, I ignored it. I clung to the fading embers of hope, praying for a miracle beep of a heart monitor, the warmth of a nurse’s hand, the return of a dream. But hope is a cruel anchor when the ship has already sunk. The years—or were they centuries?—ground me down. The silence grew teeth. The memories turned to ash. 

Loneliness is a corrosive acid. It drips onto the mind, eating away at reason, sanity, and the primal will to endure. I forgot what sunlight felt like. I forgot the taste of rain. I became a ghost haunting my own decaying consciousness, trapped in a purgatory of absolute nothingness, tethered to a body that refuses to die in a hospital bed far, far away.

Today, the silence became too loud. The void became too vast. 

I stood before the pedestal. The red light of the button pulsed like a dying heart, whispering promises of quiet, of finality, of an ultimate, unbroken sleep. 

My fingers, translucent and trembling, hovered over the plastic. I had fought so hard, for so long, guarding a spark that had long since gone cold. 

I smiled, a cracked, hollow thing, and pressed down.

The room was a cathedral of gray, vast and devoid of wind, light, or sound, save for the rhythmic, distant *hiss-click* of a lung that wasn't mine. 

For the first decade, I watched my life on an infinite loop. I played the summer afternoons in my grandfather’s orchard, the smell of bruised peaches so vivid I could almost taste them. I replayed my first heartbreak, wincing at the echoes of my own voice, and the day I graduated, feeling the phantom weight of a cardboard tube in hands I couldn't move. But memories are finite. By the twentieth year, the peach skins had turned translucent. By the thirtieth, my mother’s face had begun to blur at the edges, her smiles dissolving into static noise. 

Sanity is a fragile tether. Without friction, without new input, the mind begins to eat its own architecture. I forgot the sound of rain. I forgot the texture of denim. Eventually, I was left talking to ghosts constructed entirely of gray fog, arguing with versions of myself that no longer existed. Time lost its architecture; centuries felt like sliding down a frictionless glass slide.

And then there was the pedestal. 

It rose from the infinite mist a few paces from where my paralyzed consciousness hovered. Atop the stone pillar sat a single, matte-black console. On it, beneath a dome of cracked glass, was a thick, mechanical button. Scrawled across its surface in uneven, hand-carved letters was a single word: *END*.

For what might have been epochs, I ignored it. It was a cruel joke of the subconscious, a phantom itch I couldn’t scratch. But loneliness is a corrosive acid. It strips away pride, fear, and the instinct for self-preservation, leaving behind only the desperate, whimpering desire for a full stop. 

Every time the memories looped and faltered—when my sister's wedding became just a smear of white pixels and a hollow roar—the button pulsed with a faint, amber glow. *Come on,* it seemed to whisper through the dead air. *Turn off the television.*

Today, the last clear memory of my daughter’s laugh finally fractured into unintelligible white noise. The archive was empty. The theater was dark. 

I drifted forward, the gray mist parting before me. I didn't have fingers, but I had intention. I reached out with the ghost of a hand and pressed the button down. 

There was no explosion, no flash of light. Just a long, heavy, satisfying mechanical *click*, followed by the sound of a very old machine finally, mercifully, powering down.

Time ceased to be a river long ago; here, it was a stagnant ocean, heavy and suffocating. I floated within it as a disembodied consciousness, anchored only by a glowing, monolithic pedestal rising from the gray abyss. Atop the pedestal rested a solitary black button, stark against the marble. Engraved upon its surface was a single word: END.

Beside the button flickered the Archive—my life, projected in infinite, looping reels. For the first few subjective decades, I indulged in the ghosts of my past. I watched myself run through sun-dappled autumn leaves, laughed at echoes of forgotten jokes, and wept over the warmth of embraces I could no longer feel. I was both the audience and the actor, condemned to haunt the museum of my own existence.

But eternity is a corrosive thing. 

As the centuries—or perhaps mere seconds—bled together, the memories began to rot. The sun-dappled leaves turned to ash. Laughter devolved into shrieking cacophony. Faces of loved ones smeared into featureless, weeping clay. I re-watched my first kiss a million times until the affection dissolved, leaving behind only mechanical geometry. By the time I had processed every heartbeat of my thirty years of waking life for the ten-thousandth time, the Archive was no longer a comfort. It was a torture chamber of decaying echoes.

Then came the loneliness. It was a physical weight, pressing against my fragile sanity, threatening to crush the last remnants of my identity. I tried to speak, but my voice had no air. I tried to scream, but the silence swallowed it whole. I was an island of thought in a dead cosmos, slowly, agonizingly unravelling at the seams. My mind fractured into jagged shards, each piece screaming in unison against the quiet.

My gaze drifted back to the pedestal. The button glowed with a soft, inviting pulse. 

For ages, I resisted it, clinging stubbornly to the flickering wreckage of my memories. But the erosion was complete. There was nothing left to preserve, nothing left to feel except the agonizing stretch of forever. 

I reached out with a hand of pure will. The gray mist parted. The looping reels of my ruined life flickered out, plunging the abyss into true, absolute darkness. 

My phantom finger pressed down. 

The silence shattered. For the first time in an age, I felt something—a sudden, rushing descent, a swift unravelling, and finally, blessedly, nothing at all.

To whoever finds this, if hands still reach for stars and minds still wonder in the dark, greetings. 

My name is Elena. I am the last. 

For months, the silence of the cities has been my only companion. The great engines of the world have sputtered and died, left behind by the Red Rust, a synthetic plague that outlived its creators. It spares neither the young nor the old, neither the kings nor the beggars. In three days, perhaps four, my blood will turn as quiet as the streets outside my window. Before the fever takes my final breath, I feel a pressing need to leave a monument—not of stone, which time grinds to dust, but of thought. 

You are likely looking at the ruins of our civilization with confusion. You see skeletal skyscrapers piercing the clouds, rusting metal beasts lining overgrown highways, and oceans choked with the plastics of our transient triumphs. You will wonder who we were, and why we vanished so completely. 

We were a contradiction. We were a species capable of splitting the fundamental building blocks of the universe, yet we could not bridge the divides in our own hearts. We built telescopes that peered back to the dawn of time, and weapons that could have unmade it. We were fiercely, beautifully, tragically alive. 

We loved things that did not last. We wrote songs about the fleeting nature of spring, painted sunsets that made our chests ache, and wept when our pets grew old. We spent our brief, burning decades searching for meaning in the void, desperate to know if we were alone. 

If you are reading this, now you know the answer. We were not alone, but we missed you in the dark. 

This book is not a history of our wars, nor a blueprint of our science. Those are dead things, and they are better left buried. Instead, on the pages that follow, I have tried to capture the texture of being human. I have written of the taste of rain, the warmth of a lover’s hand, the sharp sting of grief, and the quiet, stubborn hope that made us look up at the night sky and reach out. 

Do not pity us too much. We laughed, we wept, we danced under dying stars, and for a brief, blinding moment, we owned the world. 

Look after it. 

— Elena, of Earth

To whoever finds this, if you possess eyes to read and a mind to wonder, greetings. 

My name is Arthur Pendelton. As of this morning, I am the final member of my species. The fever reached my lungs three days ago, and according to the rapid progression of the pathogen, I have perhaps seventy-two hours before my heart stops beating entirely. There are no hospitals left, no doctors, and no survivors in the neighboring ruins. I am utterly, singularly alone.

I am writing this on the back of an old laminated map of the world, using a thick black marker that refuses to bleed through the cheap paper. It is the only medium I could find that will outlast me. When the others—the ships in the sky, or the creatures of the deep earth, or whatever intelligence eventually inherits this overgrown, silent blue marble—arrive, I want you to know that we were here. We were not ghosts, and we were not gods. We were simply people.

We built towers of steel and glass that pierced the clouds, yet we could not conquer a microscopic strand of rogue proteins. We mapped the stars, split the atom, and composed symphonies that could make a grown man weep, yet we spent half our history tearing each other apart over borders drawn in the dirt. We were brilliant, and we were catastrophically foolish.

If you are looking at our empty cities, our rusted cars, and our overgrown highways, do not pity us too deeply. We lived fiercely. We loved with an intensity that defied our short lifespans, we laughed in the dark, and we dreamed of the very cosmos that you likely now call home. We painted the walls of caves, and then we painted the face of the moon. 

My hands are shaking now, the fever climbing higher. The ink is beginning to blur. Turn the page if you wish to see how we ate, how we played, and how we loved. But first, know this: we were magnificent, even if we burned out too fast.

My hands shake as I lower the fountain pen onto the virgin parchment. This is the last heavy notebook in the library, salvaged from a world that forgot how to write with anything other than glowing glass. Outside, the wind howls through the hollow canyons of Manhattan, carrying the grey dust of eight billion ghosts. I have three days left, perhaps four, before the red fever liquefies my organs and joins me to the silence.

They will come eventually. Not tomorrow, and perhaps not for a thousand winters, but the stars are too crowded for Earth to remain empty forever. Whoever you are—beings of silicon, creatures of liquid methane, or winged things born under a distant sun—listen. Do not judge us by our weapons, which still rust in underground silos, nor by the poisoned oceans we leave behind. 

Judge us by the music. 

We were a species of staggering contradictions. We split the atom and built cathedrals to capture the light of stained glass. We wept over stray dogs and waged wars that blotted out the sun. We were terribly afraid of the dark, and yet we flew into it, leaving our footprints in the gray dust of a dead moon. We loved sunsets, the taste of salt on skin, the inexplicable joy of a minor-key melody, and the desperate hope that we were never truly alone in the vast, indifferent machine of the cosmos.

I am Arthur, and I am the final page of a very long, very messy book. I sit by a window of cracked glass, watching the autumn leaves drift down through a sky that has forgotten the sound of human laughter. As I write this, my chest tightens, and the fever whispers at the edge of my consciousness. 

Turn the page. Let me tell you about the morning we discovered fire, and how we spent every day since trying to put it out, or keep it warm. Let me tell you about what it meant to be alive.

Arthur stared at the laminated contract, his index finger tracing the bold, unyielding font. *You will be given $1 million if and only if you can staple Jello to a wall.* 

Across the mahogany table, Mr. Henderson, a lawyer with the cold, dead eyes of an accountant who loved loopholes, clicked his ballpoint pen. "Those are the terms, Mr. Pendelton. No tricks. Just Jello. A wall. And a standard office stapler."

Arthur swallowed hard. One million dollars. It was enough to pay off his crushing medical debt, buy a modest house, and finally stop eating generic-brand ramen. "And the Jello has to be… out of the box? Prepared?"

"The state of the gelatin is entirely up to you," Henderson replied smoothly. "So long as it adheres to that drywall via mechanical fasteners."

Twenty-four hours later, Arthur’s kitchen looked like a crime scene involving a fluorescent strawberry. He had consulted physicists, bakers, and a deeply confused man at a local hardware store. Standard Jello, he quickly learned, was basically colored water locked in a fragile molecular matrix. A staple—even a heavy-duty Swingline—would slice right through it, leaving a weeping red crater while the rest of the dessert collapsed into a sad, quivering puddle on the floor. 

He needed reinforcement. 

Arthur’s second attempt involved wood glue and gelatin. A disaster. Attempt three: cross-stitching gelatin with fishing wire before stapling. The tension snapped the Jello in half. 

With only hours left before the deadline, desperation gave way to madness. Arthur raided the pantry. He boiled water, but instead of the recommended two cups, he used two tablespoons. Then, he added three packets of unflavored industrial-grade gelatin, a box of cornstarch, and, for reasons he couldn't fully articulate, a generous squeeze of Gorilla Glue. 

He poured the molten brick-in-waiting into a shallow aluminum pan and shoved it into the freezer. 

At noon the next day, Henderson stood in Arthur’s hallway, tapping his wristwatch. Arthur pulled the pan from the freezer. What emerged was no longer a dessert. It was a translucent, ruby-red slab of high-density polymer, cold enough to frost the surrounding air. 

With trembling hands, Arthur raised the red brick against the drywall. He grabbed the stapler. He pressed it flush against the gelatin, closed his eyes, and slammed his palm down twice. 

*Clack. Clack.*

Arthur opened his eyes. Two silver staples pierced the ruby mass, biting deep into the wooden stud behind the drywall. The Jello didn’t bleed. It didn’t quiver. It hung there, defying the laws of culinary physics.

The snow fell in thick, silent curtains, burying the sounds of the war five miles south. Around the small iron stove, four men of the 4th Infantry huddled, their uniforms stiff with frozen mud and dried blood. They had deserted before the artillery barrage turned the valley to ash. Here, beneath the towering pines, the world felt mercifully dead.

Private Miller stared into the red glow of the stove’s open hatch. "Hear that?"

"Just the wind," muttered Corporal Hayes, not looking up from his whetstone. The rhythmic scrape of steel on metal was the only sound besides the hissing snow.

"No," Miller whispered. "It’s... regular."

It was. Through the howl of the blizzard came a low, pulsing thrum, like a giant heart beating deep beneath the permafrost. The pine trees shivered, though the air above was dead calm. 

Then came the light. 

It didn't emanate from a flashlight or a flare. It rose from the snow itself—a pale, violet luminescence seeping upward from the roots of the trees. The snow crystals shifted, self-assembling into intricate, jagged geometry that defied the wind. 

Vance, the youngest of them, dropped his tin cup. The coffee didn’t spill; it froze solid in mid-air, defying gravity. 

"Pack up," Hayes rasped, his voice cracking. He stood, grabbing his rifle, but his boots were sinking. The earth beneath them had turned soft and viscous, like warm flesh. 

The forest was changing. The dark trunks of the pines began to stretch, warping into elongated, rib-like arches that leaned inward over the camp. From the violet light below, silhouettes began to rise—dozens of them, tall and impossibly thin, gliding silently over the drifts. They wore no coats, and their skin possessed the translucent sheen of river ice. They bore no weapons, only hollow, weeping sockets where eyes should have been.

Miller screamed, backing away until his spine hit a tree. The tree groaned—a wet, organic sound—and wrapped thick, bark-covered tendrils around his shoulders, pinning him fast. 

"Don't look!" Hayes shouted, firing his rifle blindly into the dark. The muzzle flash cast stark, violent shadows, but the bullets made no sound when they struck the approaching figures. They simply passed through, as if shooting smoke.

The coldest air imaginable rushed into the clearing, stealing the breath from their lungs. The entities surrounded them, their movements fluid and coordinated, like dancers beneath a frozen sea. One drifted toward Vance, lifting a long, pale finger to touch the boy’s temple. 

Vance’s eyes rolled back. When he spoke, his voice was echoed by a hundred overlapping whispers from the frost. 

"The metal," Vance said, his face slack. "You brought the metal here. The iron. The lead. It wakes the sleepers."

The stove hissed and went pitch black. The violet light flared blindingly bright, consuming the trees, the snow, and the men in a silent, freezing flash. 

By morning, the woodland was empty. There were no boot prints, no camp, and no blood. Just a perfect circle of melted earth, where the snow refused to fall.

*December 24, 1944.*

The Ardennes were a suffocating kind of quiet. Miles away from the artillery thudding against the freezing earth, our little tent sat nestled in the shadow of pines heavy with unblemished snow. Four of us huddled around a stove that gave off more smoke than heat. Miller was cleaning his rifle, the metallic *clack-clink* the only sound cutting through the howling wind outside. 

Then, the wind stopped. 

It wasn't a gradual dying down. One second the canvas was snapping wildly, and the next, absolute, tomb-like stillness. Even the crackle of the wood stove muffled itself. 

"You hear that?" Vane asked, his voice a dry rasp. He stopped chewing on his hardtack, eyes darting to the tent flap. 

"The weather broke," Miller muttered, though he didn't look up. 

"No," Corporal Hayes said, setting his mug down. "It’s too quiet. Even the woods... the woods are dead."

We all felt it then. A drop in temperature so sharp my breath instantly frosted into thick plumes. The lantern light flickered, stretching our shadows against the canvas—not outward toward the walls, but inward, pooling unnaturally at our boots. 

Then came the footsteps. 

*Crunch. Crunch. Crunch.*

Heavy, deliberate strides moving through the deep snow outside. They weren't marching boots; they lacked the rhythmic cadence of soldiers. They sounded heavy, unhurried, dragging something massive behind them. 

Miller raised his M1, safety clicking off with a loud, echoing snap. "Halt! Who goes there? Password!" he shouted toward the canvas. 

The footsteps stopped right outside our door. 

Nobody answered. Instead, the shadows on the tent floor began to twist. They detached from our bodies, writhing and stretching independently toward the entrance. 

"Get your weapons!" Hayes yelled, scrambling for his carbine. 

Before any of us could fire, the flap blew open—not inward from a gust of wind, but ripped entirely off its moorings by an invisible force. 

There was no man standing there. Just a thick, swirling mist that smelled violently of ozone, pine needles, and copper. From the center of the fog, two glowing, amber eyes opened, staring directly into my soul. They weren't angry eyes; they were ancient, starving, and entirely devoid of human reason.

Miller fired. The muzzle flash illuminated the tent in a blinding white glare, but the bullets simply vanished the moment they entered the mist, swallowed by the dark. 

Vane screamed, a high, ragged sound, as his own shadow lunged up and wrapped cold, spectral hands around his throat. He clawed at empty air, his face turning purple before he slumped forward, entirely lifeless, though no physical wound marked his skin. 

I scrambled backward until my spine hit the frozen ground, clutching my rifle like a talisman. The amber eyes turned to me, tilting sideways with an unnatural, bone-snapping crack. 

*Not yet,* a voice echoed, not in my ears, but vibrating directly inside my skull—heavy like sliding glaciers. *The dark is wide. We will wait.*

The fog vanished. The wind slammed back into the clearing with the force of a freight train, and the stove roared back to life. 

I sat shaking in the freezing dark, staring at Vane’s cold body, listening to the distant, muffled booms of a war that suddenly felt entirely insignificant.

December 14th. Snow falls thick and silent in the pines, burying the distant thunder of the artillery miles to the west. Here, deep in the timber, four of us share a meager fire. Corporal Vance tends the kettle, while Miller and young Jensen shiver in their overcoats. 

We are deserters, though none of us say the word aloud. We just walked away from the trenches when the shelling grew too loud, seeking only a quiet place to freeze. 

The forest is too quiet. That is what bothers me first. Even the wind seems to hold its breath. The snow falling around us doesn't drift; it drops in straight, heavy lines, absorbing the crackle of our dying fire until the flames make no sound at all.

"Hear that?" Jensen whispers, his spoon clinking against his tin cup. 

"Just the wind, kid," Vance mutters, though his eyes dart to the treeline. 

It isn't the wind. Between the trunks, the darkness shifts. It possesses no shape, yet it moves with purpose, a crawling shadow bleeding out from the roots of the ancient hemlocks. The fire sputters, turning from a warm amber to a sickly, cobalt blue. The temperature plunges instantly, our breath pluming in violent, frost-bitten clouds. 

"Put it out," Miller chokes, scrambling backward into the snow. "Put it out!"

Vance kicks snow over the embers, plunging us into absolute blackness—save for the woods. 

The trees are glowing. Not with light, but with a pale, phosphorescent frost that outlines the bark in glowing, geometric patterns. And then, the forest floor begins to breathe. The earth heaves beneath us, a slow, rhythmic pulse as if we are resting on the chest of a buried titan. 

Footsteps ring out in the snow. Heavy boots. Marching in perfect, dreadful synchronization. *Crunch. Crunch. Crunch.* They are circling our camp, just beyond the reach of the glowing pines. 

Jensen whimpers, pressing his face into his knees. The invisible soldiers march closer. I can smell them—not the stench of gunpowder and rot from the battlefield, but the copper tang of fresh blood and the bitter chill of a winter grave. 

A voice cuts through the cold, speaking in no language I know, yet echoing directly inside my skull. It is a command, heavy with finality. 

Vance stands up, his eyes wide and milky white. He doesn't look at us. He walks straight into the glowing darkness, swallowed by the shadows without a sound. 

"Vance?" Miller cries out, reaching forward. 

Another set of footsteps approaches. Miller stands next, his movements robotic, joining the unseen ranks. 

Jensen is hyperventilating, sobbing in the dark. I grab his collar, but my fingers close on thin air. He is already standing. 

Alone in the freezing dark, the rhythmic marching stops. The weight of a thousand unseen eyes presses down on my chest, demanding I fall in line. I close my eyes, step forward into the snow, and take my place in the silent ranks.

It started on a Tuesday in October. Not with a moral awakening, but with a pigeon and a leaf blower. 

I was working my after-school job at the local garden center, a place whose primary demographic was retirees with too much time and an aggressive hatred of dandelions. My boss, Greg, a man whose personality was entirely composed of sawdust and Marlboro Reds, told me to clear the back parking lot. 

So, I fired up the backpack leaf blower. It was a glorious, rumbling monster of internal combustion that smelled like sweet-and-sour exhaust and deafened you to the miserable realities of suburban existence. I felt like a god of autumn. I swept the red and gold leaves into neat, obedient piles. 

Then, I saw it. A pigeon. Not a majestic bird of prey, but a feathered rat with a crippled foot, sitting dead center in my path. 

Any normal, well-adjusted teenager would have turned off the machine, nudged it aside, and gone back to minimum wage. But I was seventeen, sleep-deprived, and fueled entirely by three-day-old iced coffee and existential dread. I made a choice. An ethical dilemma of monumental proportions. 

I revved the engine. 

The pigeon did not fly. It puffed out its chest, lowered its head, and accepted its fate. It looked at me with the ancient, unblinking disdain of a creature that had survived millennia of human stupidity and city buses. It was a staring contest between adolescent apathy and urban avian resilience. 

I didn't blow it away. I stood there for four full minutes, holding a fifty-pound jet engine on my back, locked in a silent philosophical debate with a bird. 

What did it teach me? Nothing. It taught me that life is absurd, that authority figures like Greg don't care about philosophical poultry, and that sometimes, the most profound thing you can do is just stand still while the world screams around you. 

Please accept me into your prestigious institution. Or don't. Either way, the pigeon is still out there, and so am I.

Arthur stared at his translucent hands, a sudden, cold fury washing over him. "So where is he? The guy wearing my life?"

Peter pointed a thumb down the massive staircase winding into the misty abyss. "Well, since he technically used your name to enter paradise, and the clerical error hasn't been ironed out by heavenly HR... he’s currently reclining in a velvet-upholstered VIP suite on the Upper Tier."

Arthur gripped the lapels of his spectral suit. "Give me a map, Peter. Nobody steals Arthur Pendelton's afterlife. If I'm going to purgatory, I'm taking my credit rating back."

The ethereal glow of the Pearly Gates was breathtaking, gleaming like polished mother-of-pearl against a backdrop of infinite twilight. I stood there, dusting invisible ash from my spectral trousers, expecting trumpets, or at least a warm smile from a cherub. 

Instead, a burly archangel with an impeccably trimmed beard and a glowing digital clipboard sighed, blocking my path.

"Name?" he asked, not looking up.

"Arthur Pendelton," I replied, standing up straight. "Heart attack. Third cup of espresso on a Tuesday. Not my finest moment."

The archangel tapped the screen. A holographic projection unfurled, displaying a sprawling, highly flattering dossier. "Arthur Pendelton. Born 1984. Accountant. Donated twenty bucks to public radio in 2012. Ah, yes. Right this way, Mr. Pendelton—"

He stopped. His brow furrowed. He tapped the glass harder. The screen flickered, flashed crimson, and emitted a polite, deeply judgmental chime.

"Wait," the archangel muttered. He squinted at me, then at the tablet, then back at me. "Hold on a second. You're Arthur Pendelton?"

"Yes?" I said, suddenly feeling very underdressed for eternity.

"That's weird," the angel said, pressing an intercom button. "Gabriel, get down here. We’ve got a duplicate glitch in Sector Four."

Another winged entity materialized, sipping from a mug that read *World’s Okayest Seraph*. "What's the issue?"

"This guy claims he's Arthur Pendelton," the first angel said, pointing at me like I was a rogue stain on a heavenly rug. "The accountant from Ohio. Moderate tipper. Mildly pious."

"Impossible," Gabriel said, leaning over the tablet. "Arthur Pendelton checked in twenty minutes ago. Total saint. Built orphanages in his spare time, rescued three golden retrievers from a burning building, wrote poetry that made God cry."

I blinked. "I mostly play video games and yell at people who don't use their blinkers."

"See?" Gabriel pointed at me. "The guy inside is currently receiving his wings and a customized halo. Meanwhile, you're standing here looking like you died of chronic sarcasm."

A cold, terrifying dread washed over my non-existent stomach. "Wait. Are you telling me someone stole my identity?"

"It appears," the archangel said dryly, "that an enterprising soul hijacked your social security number, your moral ledger, and your entire earthly existence, speed-running virtue right under your nose."

I stared at the glowing golden gates, listening to the faint sound of harp music and applause echoing from the VIP lounge where Fake Arthur was undoubtedly receiving a lifetime achievement award. 

"So," I said, rubbing my temples. "Does this mean I go to hell?"

Gabriel checked his tablet. "Well, according to your *actual* file, you once stole a pack of gum in 1999 and never apologized." He looked up, offering a sympathetic wince. "Hope you like sulfur."

Arthur Pendelton’s last memory was the blinding headlights of a semi-truck on Interstate 95. His next was standing before towering gates of iridescent pearl, feeling remarkably light and entirely dead. 

An angel with immaculate silver wings and a pair of heavy, wire-rimmed spectacles sat behind a polished cloud-desk, diligently tapping away on a keyboard made of crystallized light. 

"Name?" the angel asked without looking up.

"Arthur Pendelton," Arthur replied, clearing a throat that no longer needed clearing.

The angel’s fingers paused. He adjusted his glasses, peered over them, and tapped a few more keys. A massive holographic ledger materialized in the air between them. The angel frowned, his halo dipping slightly to the left. 

"Well, Mr. Pendelton," the angel said, his voice echoing softly. "According to my records, you died five years ago in a hang-gliding accident in Ibiza."

Arthur blinked. "That’s impossible. I’ve never even been to Spain. I hate heights. I died ten minutes ago in a truck crash."

The angel sighed, a sound like a gentle autumn breeze rustling through dry leaves. "Sir, people try to bluff their way past me all the time. Usually, they claim to be saints or philanthropists. Identity fraud at the Pearly Gates is a new one."

"I am not committing fraud!" Arthur protested, throwing his hands up. "Look at me! I'm Arthur Pendelton! Social Security number ending in 4482, born in Cincinnati, allergic to shellfish!"

The angel checked the screen again. A strange expression crossed his celestial face. He tapped the desk three times, and a file stamped with a fiery red *‘PENDING’* appeared. 

"That’s odd," the angel murmured. "The Ibiza Arthur Pendelton checked in with a verified digital signature, a complete biometric scan, and a lifetime ledger of moderately good deeds. But his physical description... well, he claimed to be six-foot-two with a full head of hair."

"I'm five-foot-eight and bald!" Arthur shouted, his blood pressure briefly spiking despite his lack of a circulatory system. 

The angel leaned back, stroking his chin. "It appears someone stole your identity while you were alive. They assumed your credit score, emptied your 401(k), and apparently, beat you to the afterlife. They used your remaining grace credits to secure a premium suite in the Elysian Fields."

Arthur stood frozen in the celestial mist, a profound sense of cosmic injustice washing over him. "So... what happens to me?"

The angel offered an apologetic smile and handed him a clipboard. "Well, technically, you don’t exist on our books anymore. But we do have an opening in Purgatory’s administrative archives. The pay is terrible, but the coffee is surprisingly good."

Arthur adjusted his woolen scarf, fighting a losing battle against the biting November wind. His joints throbbed with the cold, his boss had just informed him that his pension was vanishing into a corporate restructuring, and on his walk home from the bus stop, a passing SUV had drenched him from ankle to hip in slush. 

He slumped onto the damp wooden bench of the deserted bus shelter, buried his face in his red-raw hands, and let out a shuddering sigh. 

"Life's a bitch," Arthur muttered to the empty air. 

"You've no idea," a deep, surprisingly warm voice replied. 

Arthur jumped, looking up. Sitting on the other end of the bench was a tall, impeccably dressed man in a charcoal-grey overcoat. He was wearing a tasteful silk scarf and sipping from a paper cup that radiated faint wisps of steam. 

"Excuse me?" Arthur said, wiping rain from his eyes. 

"I said, you've no idea," the man repeated, offering a sympathetic smile that crinkled the corners of his kind, dark eyes. "Though, to be fair, you're experiencing it firsthand. Or, well, *she* is handing it to you firsthand."

Arthur frowned. "Who are you?"

"Name’s Mort," the man said, extending a gloved hand. 

Arthur hesitated, then shook it. The stranger’s hand was cool, but comforting, like pressing your palm against a glass of iced water on a sweltering July afternoon. "Arthur."

"I know," Mort said gently. He reached into the deep pocket of his coat and produced a second paper cup, holding it out. "Peppermint tea. It helps with the chill. And the existential dread."

Arthur took it, murmuring a confused thank you. He took a sip. It was sweet, hot, and instantly chased the ice from his chest. 

"So," Mort said, leaning back and watching the sleet dance in the glow of the streetlamp. "Job troubles? Health acting up? The universe treating you like a piñata?"

"All of the above," Arthur sighed, resting his head against the shelter's glass wall. "Sometimes I wonder why I even bother getting up in the morning. It’s just one indignity after another."

"She’s exhausting, isn't she?" Mort mused, taking a sip of his own drink. 

"Who?"

"Life," Mort said, gesturing vaguely with his cup. "High maintenance. Mood swings. Incredible highs, sure, but the lows? My word. She thrives on the drama. Heartbreak, taxes, stubbing your toe on the coffee table at three in the morning. She loves it."

Arthur gave a hollow, wet chuckle. "You sound like you know her."

"We used to be close," Mort said softly. "Dated for a few millennia. But we grew apart. She’s too high-strung. Always needing to *happen*, always rushing around. Me? I prefer peace and quiet."

Arthur squinted at the stranger. The man’s dark coat seemed to absorb the neon light of the city, and the air around him smelled faintly of autumn leaves and old, leather-bound books. A sudden, cold realization washed over Arthur. 

"Wait," Arthur whispered. "You're...?"

Mort turned his head, offering a gentle, reassuring smile. "Yeah."

Arthur froze. His mind raced through a dozen frantic questions, but strangely, panic didn't take root. Instead, a profound, heavy fatigue settled over his shoulders. He looked down at his soaked shoes, then out at the miserable, swirling grey city. 

"Are you here for me?" Arthur asked quietly. 

"Not yet," Mort said, resting a warm hand on Arthur’s trembling shoulder. "Not for a good thirty years, if you play your cards right. Eat less sodium, call your sister."

Arthur let out a breath he felt like he’d been holding for sixty years. "Is it peaceful?"

"The absolute best," Mort said, his eyes crinkling. "No rush hour. No bills. Just a quiet room, a comfortable chair, and all the time in the world to read, or sleep, or just *be*."

Mort finished his tea, crumpled the paper cup, and stood up, smoothing the front of his coat. 

"Well," Mort said, tipping an imaginary hat. "I've got a busy night ahead. A few strokes in the ICU, an old dog in Brooklyn. You know how it is."

"Wait," Arthur said, looking up as the stranger stepped toward the curb. "Life's a bitch."

Mort paused, looking back over his shoulder with a knowing, gentle grin. 

"And Death?" Arthur asked, a faint, genuine smile touching his own lips. 

"Well," Death said, winking. "Death is actually a pretty nice guy."

Then, with the soft rustle of falling leaves, he was gone. 

Arthur sat alone in the shelter for a moment longer. The wind was still howling, and his shoes were still soaked. But as he took another sip of the peppermint tea, the cold didn't seem quite so sharp anymore.

"Life's a bitch and Death... Well Death is actually a pretty nice guy."

That was what my grandfather always said, usually right before he took a long sip of whiskey and stared blankly at the rain-streaked window. I never really understood what he meant until the night my apartment caught fire.

It started with a faulty toaster, a cheap plastic appliance that finally decided to end its miserable existence by turning my kitchen into an inferno. By the time I woke up, the smoke was thick, acrid, and choking. I stumbled toward the door, coughing violently, only to trip over my own rug and smash my head against the coffee table. 

Darkness rushed in. 

When I opened my eyes, I wasn't in a hospital, and I wasn't dead in the traditional, heavenly-cloud kind of way. I was sitting at a small, round diner table checkered in red and white. A soft, neon 'Open' sign buzzed gently in the window, casting a warm pink glow over the room. Outside, there was just an endless, comforting gray fog.

"Rough night, huh?" 

I jumped. Sitting across from me was a tall, slender man wearing a sharp tweed suit. He had kind, crinkling eyes behind thin wire-rimmed glasses, and a salt-and-pepper beard that made him look like a friendly college professor. On the table between us sat two mugs of steaming coffee and a plate of warm chocolate chip cookies.

"Am I...?" I stammered, rubbing the sore spot on my forehead.

"Dead? Yes. Well and truly," the man said warmly, sliding the plate of cookies toward me. "Help yourself. They're fresh. Well, as fresh as things get around here."

I stared at him, bewildered. "Who are you?"

"The name's Arthur," he said, extending a hand. I took it automatically; his grip was firm and reassuring. "And before you ask, no, I don't have a scythe. Honestly, who even uses scythes anymore? Terrible ergonomics. Back pain for days."

"Arthur?" I blinked. "Like... the Grim Reaper?"

He chuckled, a rich, soothing sound. "That’s the marketing department's doing, not mine. 'The Grim Reaper.' Honestly, it's so dramatic. People panic when they hear it. But think about it: Life gets you up at dawn, hands you a mountain of bills, makes your car break down on the freeway, and gives you a cold right when you have a big presentation. Life is a relentless, exhausting taskmaster."

He took a gentle sip of his coffee. 

"Me? I just sit down, offer a warm beverage, and listen. No spreadsheets. No taxes. Just a quiet chat before the next leg of the journey."

I looked down at the coffee, then at the half-eaten cookie in my trembling hand. For the first time in years, my chest didn't feel tight with anxiety. 

"You know what?" I whispered, taking a bite of the cookie. "My grandfather was right."

Arthur’s final Tuesday on Earth began when he slipped on a rogue frozen pea, cracked his skull against the edge of a vintage radiator, and launched his soul unceremoniously out of his body. 

He groaned, hovering above his pathetic, cardigan-clad corpse. Life’s a bitch, he thought bitterly, replaying the indignities of his fifty-eight years: the crippling student debt, the divorce that cost him his beloved record collection, the chronic sciatica, and finally, dying because he couldn't be bothered to sweep the kitchen floor. 

"You can say that again," a smooth, baritone voice sighed beside him.

Arthur spun around. Sitting on the arm of his worn-out armchair was a remarkably well-dressed gentleman in a sharply tailored charcoal suit. He had salt-and-pepper hair, warm brown eyes, and was casually filing his thumbnail. 

"Who are you?" Arthur asked, clutching his chest out of sheer habit. "Gabriel? Azrael? Are you here to drag me down to the fiery pits?"

The man chuckled, tucking the nail file away. "Goodness, no. The fiery pits are wildly overrated and the ventilation is atrocious. No, Arthur, I’m Death."

Arthur blinked, looking from the sharp suit to the lack of scythe, skeleton, or ominous dark hood. "Where's the black cloak? Where's the terror?"

"Oh, please. That's just millennia of terrible PR," Death said, standing up and dusting off his lapels. "People project their own misery onto me. They have a miserable time down there, blame it on me, and suddenly I’m public enemy number one. But Death... well, Death is actually a pretty nice guy."

Death stepped forward and offered a warm, reassuring smile. He pulled a thermos from his briefcase and unscrewed the cap, releasing the rich, heavenly aroma of freshly brewed Earl Grey tea. 

"Care for a cup before we head out?" Death asked, conjuring two porcelain mugs from thin air. 

Arthur stared at the mug, utterly bewildered. "Wait. That's it? No judgment? No lightning bolts?"

"None at all. Your ledger is a mess, frankly, but who am I to judge? We’ve all made questionable choices during our tenure in the land of the living." Death handed Arthur a mug. "Besides, my job isn't to punish. It's simply to escort. Think of me as a very polite Uber driver for the cosmos."

Arthur took a sip. It was, without a doubt, the best tea he had ever tasted. The lingering ache in his ghostly back melted away, replaced by a profound, unexpected sense of peace. He looked down at his lifeless shell on the floor, then back at the elegant gentleman offering him a comforting smile. 

"You know," Arthur said, taking another sip, "you're alright, Death."

"I try my best, Arthur. Now, shall we?" Death held out his arm. Together, the weary mortal and the surprisingly charming Reaper walked out through the living room wall, leaving all of life's bitterness far behind.

The Republic was a rotting carcass, and Rome’s streets had become its writhing maggots. Since Caesar fell beneath the daggers of cowardly liberators, the Eternal City had descended into lawlessness. Senators cowered behind villa gates while thugs and corrupt magistrates carved up the ruins.

Quintus Valerius watched it all from his dining room, sipping poisoned wine with a heavy heart. He was a wealthy man, draped in silks, but his soul sickened. The law was dead. Someone else had to be the executioner.

Deep beneath his Palatine estate, past the wine cellars, lay a forgotten vault. There, Quintus shed his senator’s toga. He strapped on hardened leather greaves, pulled a heavy tunic of interlocking iron rings over his broad chest, and cinched a gladius at his waist. Finally, he drew a cowl of dark, coarse wool over his head, its deep shadow obscuring his aristocratic features. 

To the highborn, he was Quintus the Epicurean. Tonight, in the stinking alleys of the Subura, he was the *Vindex*—the Avenger.

He stepped out into the midnight fog. The cobblestones slicked with winter rain whispered beneath his boots. Up ahead, near the crumbling arches of an abandoned granary, he heard the sharp crack of a slap and a woman’s terrified plea. 

Quintus slipped into the shadows, moving with silent, deadly grace. 

Three men, members of Clodius’s street gang, had cornered a merchant’s daughter. One held a heavy iron-studded club, laughing as he tore at the girl’s cloak. The others watched, sharpening their daggers on the damp bricks.

"Please," the girl wept.

"Quiet, little dove," the leader sneered, raising his hand again.

He never brought it down. 

A heavy hand clamped over the thug's mouth, yanking him backward into the darkness with brutal velocity. Before the other two could even draw breath, Quintus stepped into the pale moonlight. 

"Who goes—?" one started, reaching for his blade.

Quintus closed the distance in a heartbeat. He blocked a clumsy thrust with his forearm, his iron-mesh gauntlet deflecting the steel, and drove a punishing fist into the man’s solar plexus. The thug collapsed, gasping for air. 

The last standing brute swung his club in a wild arc. Quintus ducked beneath the blow, surged upward, and swept the man’s legs out from under him. The thug hit the stones hard, knocked instantly unconscious. 

Silence reclaimed the alley, save for the patter of rain and the girl’s trembling breaths. Quintus turned to her, keeping his face hidden in the cowl's deep recess. 

"Go home," his voice was a low, gravelly rasp, entirely unlike a senator's. "Tell your father the streets belong to Rome again. Not them."

Before she could speak, the *Vindex* vanished into the gloom, leaving the cowering criminals bound tightly together with heavy hemp rope. Rome was burning, but tonight, the fire had a shadow.

The dagger had not killed Rome; it had merely uncorked it. 

In the weeks following the Ides of March, the Republic bled into the gutters. Senators huddled behind spiked iron gates while the mob ruled the dark, carving fortunes from screaming widows and bloodied merchants. But Senator Marcus Valerius, draped in the heavy wool of a common plebeian cloak and wearing the bruised leather mask of a dockworker, cared little for the senate floor. He cared for the alleyways.

They called the shadow *The Wolf of the Subura*. 

Marcus ducked beneath a low-hanging canvas awning, the damp Roman air stinging his lungs. Ahead, the greasy torchlight of the Subura slums flickered against crumbling brick. He heard the muffled cry first, then the cruel laughter of Antony’s leftover thugs shaking down a spice-seller. 

"I told you, old man, the tax has doubled," a rasped voice sneered. "Pay up or feed the Tiber."

Marcus stepped out from the gloom. He didn't draw a sword—too patrician, too loud. Instead, he gripped the lead-weighted leather sap hidden in his sleeve. 

"Leave him," Marcus said, his voice deepened into a gravelly growl.

Three men turned, hands dropping to the hilts of curved daggers. The biggest one, a scarred brute missing an ear, grunted. "Another stray dog. Cut him."

The first lunged, blade flashing in the amber light. Marcus sidestepped with the effortless grace of a man raised on Greek wrestling tutors, catching the thug’s wrist and snapping it back with a sickening crunch. As the man dropped, screaming, Marcus drove his elbow into the second attacker’s solar plexus, folding him like cheap papyrus. 

The scarred leader backed away, his eyes widening beneath the torchlight. "By the gods... you're that lunatic. The vigilante."

"I am the ghost of the Republic you're gutting," Marcus murmured, closing the distance. Before the thug could shout, Marcus brought the heavy sap down against his temple. The man crumpled into the mud without a sound.

The trembling spice-seller pressed himself against the damp wall, clutching a wooden box to his chest. "Mercy, master... I have nothing left."

Marcus reached into his cloak, pulled out a heavy pouch of silver denarii—skimmed directly from corrupt grain-tolls—and pressed it into the old man’s shaking hands. 

"Rebuild your stall," Marcus said quietly. "And tell the others the streets belong to the people tonight, not the jackals."

Before the old man could stammer a blessing, Marcus dissolved back into the labyrinth of Rome’s dark veins. Dawn was still hours away, and the corrupt politicians sleeping in their marble villas had no idea that justice was no longer waiting for the courts. It was sharpening its blade in the dark.

Since the Senate House ran slick with the dictator’s blood, Rome had curdled. The triumvirs bickered over legions, and the city’s back alleys belonged to the cutthroats. Senator Lucius, once famous for his eloquence in the Forum and his delicate taste in Samian pottery, watched his republic bleed from behind locked bronze doors. But wealth, Lucius knew, bought more than oil and silk; it bought shadowed secrets.

On a moonless night, the dignified patrician stripped away his Tyrian purple. In its place, he bound his torso in boiled leather, greased a set of iron knuckles, and pulled a rough-hewn hood of coarse wool over his graying brows. To the elite, Lucius was dining on dormice; to the desperate shadows of the Subura, he became a nameless omen. 

He found his quarry near the Cloaca Maxima: Balbus, a ruthless extortionist who had been starving widow-merchants of their meager grain stalls. Two thugs were shaking down a terrified olive-seller when a heavy lead-weighted *plumbata* whistled from the dark, pinning a dagger to the dirt. 

"Yield the coin," a gravelly whisper echoed from the fog.

Balbus whipped around, drawing a shortsword. "Who goes there? Show yourself, coward!"

Lucius dropped from the top of a crumbling brick archway, landing with a muted thud. He struck before the enforcers could blink. A swift heel shattered a knee; a left hook baptized another in the filthy gutter. Balbus lunged, thrusting blindly, but Lucius sidestepped with the grace of a trained gladiator, caught the extortionist’s wrist, and twisted until bone popped. 

Balbus hit the cobblestones, whimpering. Lucius stood over him, pressing a heavy boot into the man's chest. From his tunic, Lucius pulled a heavy leather pouch—stolen from Balbus’s belt—and tossed it back to the trembling olive-seller. 

"Tell your masters," Lucius hissed, leaning close to the bleeding criminal, "that Rome is not entirely abandoned."

With a swirl of his dark cloak, the vigilante vaulted up a rain-pipe, vanishing into the labyrinth of terracotta roofs just as the watchmen’s torches rounded the corner. 

An hour later, Senator Lucius reclined on his triclinium, sipping diluted Falernian wine. His knuckles throbbed beneath his linen wraps, and a fresh bruise darkened his jaw. Yet, as he stared out the window toward the Capitol, a grim smile touched his lips. Caesar was dead, and the Republic was ashes, but in the dark, justice had found a new sword.

The chalk glowed a faint, sickly violet against the hardwood floor of the nursery. Leo, six years old and armed with a stolen box of sidewalk chalk and a half-eaten lollipop, stared intently at the squiggly pentagram he’d copied from a dusty tome in his grandfather’s study. 

He didn't want gold. He didn't want revenge on the fifth-grade bully who stole his lunch money. He just wanted someone to play with.

The bedroom air plummeted twenty degrees. Shadows detached themselves from the walls, writhing and fusing into a towering mass of obsidian scales, smoking horns, and sulfur. Red eyes, burning like dying stars, glared down from the ceiling.

"WHO DARES SUMMON MALPHAS, SCOURGE OF THE ABYSS, WEEPER OF—"

The demon’s voice shook the bunk beds, rattling the stuffed animals on the top shelf. Malphas paused, expecting the usual cowering mortal begging for a kingdom or a curse. 

Instead, a small, sticky hand reached out and offered a chewed-on, grape-flavored lollipop.

"Hi," Leo said, his big blue eyes wide and entirely devoid of fear. "Do you like dinosaurs?"

Malphas blinked. His six glowing eyes blinked in rapid succession. The smoke curling from his shoulders dissipated into a confused puff. He looked down at the child, then at the half-eaten candy, and finally at the crudely drawn circle. 

"I am a creature of eternal torment," Malphas rumbled, though the volume was significantly lower. "I feast upon the despair of the living. I do not... play with dinosaurs."

"Oh," Leo said, his smile faltering just a little. He pulled the lollipop back and licked it thoughtfully. "That's okay. We can play monsters. You can be the giant beast that destroys the city, and I'll be the brave spaceman who builds it back out of Lego."

Malphas stared. Millennia of summonings had brought him greedy kings, vengeful lovers, and desperate warlords. No one had ever asked him to play. The silence stretched in the dimly lit room, broken only by the hum of the refrigerator downstairs.

With a heavy sigh that smelled faintly of brimstone, the towering demon shifted. His terrifying form began to shrink, scales smoothing over, horns retreating into his skull, until he stood as a scruffy, pale-skinned boy with pointed ears and slate-gray hair. 

"I suppose," Malphas muttered, crossing his arms awkwardly, "the city could use some destruction. But I get to be the red Lego brick."

Leo’s face lit up like a supernova. He grabbed the demon by a surprisingly cold, leathery hand and dragged him toward the giant plastic tub in the corner. 

For the first time in ten thousand years, the Scourge of the Abyss smiled, and for the rest of the afternoon, the underworld felt very far away.

Nine-year-old Toby dragged a heavy stick of chalk across the basement floor, meticulously finishing the heptagram. He’d found the summoning ritual wedged between two dusty encyclopedias in his grandfather’s attic, hidden away like a dirty secret. According to the faded parchment, the spell required three drops of blood, a pinch of sulfur, and a deep, burning desire. 

Toby pricked his finger with a pushpin, squeezed three crimson beads onto the center of the geometric pattern, and tossed a matchbook sulfur strip onto the floor. 

"I call upon the dweller of the abyss!" Toby whispered, his voice trembling slightly. "Hear my plea!"

The basement air grew instantly frigid. Shadows pooled in the corners, stretching and writhing as if waking from a long sleep. The concrete floor cracked with a sound like pistol shots, and a thick plume of black smoke billowed upward, smelling of ozone and ancient ash. Two glowing yellow eyes pierced through the haze, followed by massive, obsidian horns and leathery shoulders.

*MORTAL,* a voice like grinding tectonic plates echoed directly inside Toby’s skull. *YOU DARE SUMMON MALPHAS, THE SCOURGE OF THE SEVENTH HELL? SPEAK YOUR DESIRE. DO YOU SEEK WEALTH? VENGEANCE? THE DESTRUCTION OF YOUR ENEMIES?*

Toby blinked, clutching a worn-out stuffed bear to his chest. He looked up at the terrifying, seven-foot-tall entity of pure nightmare fuel. 

"Do you want to play Mario Kart?" Toby asked.

Malphas froze. The flames dancing along his massive horns flickered and died. The terrifying aura of dread evaporated, replaced by an awkward, bewildered silence. 

*...What?* the demon thought-spoke, the terrifying resonance entirely gone, replaced by a tone of utter confusion.

"Mario Kart," Toby repeated, holding up a grey Nintendo 64 cartridge. "On the TV over there. My older brother went to high school, and my mom says I'm too young to play online with strangers, and nobody at school likes me because I have weird teeth. So... I summoned someone."

Malphas stared at the small boy. He looked down at his own enormous, razor-sharp claws, entirely unsuited for holding a standard controller. He thought of the endless lakes of fire, the eternal wailing of the damned, and the soul-crushing paperwork he had been buried under for the last six hundred years. 

Slowly, the towering demon crouched down, the concrete groaning beneath his weight. The terrifying red glow in his eyes softened to a warm amber. 

*...Can I be Yoshi?* Malphas asked. 

Toby smiled, a gap-toothed grin. "Only if I get to be Bowser."

Seven-year-old Toby dragged a stick of bright red sidewalk chalk across his bedroom floor, meticulously drawing a triangle inside a circle. The dusty velvet of his mother’s old sewing room had provided the candles, and his favorite picture book had provided the instructions. He didn’t want gold, and he didn’t want revenge on the fifth-grade bullies. Toby just wanted a playmate who wouldn’t cheat at Mario Kart.

He pricked his finger with a pushpin, squeezed a single crimson drop onto the center of the diagram, and cleared his throat. Reading the faux-Latin runes from the crinkled paper, he whispered, "Come forth, Malphast, Lord of the Ash."

The bedroom temperature plummeted. Shadows detached themselves from the corners, writhing and twisting until they solidified into a towering figure with obsidian skin, curving ram horns, and eyes like molten brass. The air smelled of sulfur and ozone.

Malphast straightened to his full, terrifying height, his voice shaking the floorboards. "WHO DARES SUMMON THE HARVESTER OF—" He paused, blinking yellow eyes down at the small boy sitting cross-legged in mismatched dinosaur pajamas. "Wait. You're tiny."

"I'm seven," Toby said, holding up seven sticky fingers. "Well, almost eight."

The demon crossed massive, clawed arms, looking thoroughly bewildered. "Where are the virgin sacrifices? The weeping maidens? Do you have any idea how much paperwork I had to bypass to get up here from the Ninth Pit?"

"I have half a juice box," Toby offered, sliding a carton of apple punch across the rug. "And some fruit snacks."

Malphast stared at the carton, then down at the chalk drawing. "This is a binding circle. You trapped me."

"I had to, or you wouldn't stay," Toby explained earnestly. "Everyone at school is mean, and my big brother only plays with his friends. I just wanted someone to build Legos with. My name is Toby."

Silence hung heavily in the bedroom, broken only by the hum of the refrigerator downstairs. The demon looked at the towering heap of colorful plastic bricks in the corner, then back at the boy. The terrifying aura of brimstone slowly flickered out, replaced by a faint, confused sigh. 

"Legos," Malphast muttered, pinching the bridge of his scaly nose. "I command legions of damned souls. I wage eternal war in the obsidian wastes." He looked at the tiny red dragon Toby held out. "Is that a fire-breathing beast?"
